title: Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching

paper.title: Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching
paper.abstract:
Abstract We propose Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching (CCVFM), a
generative model that augments hierarchical rectified flow with a
data-informed source distribution. Hierarchical flow matching models
the full conditional velocity law in velocity space, but its inner
flow is asked to transport isotropic Gaussian noise to a multimodal
target velocity distribution from scratch. Our key observation is that this inner source can
be replaced by a closed-form surrogate built from a coreset of the
target. CCVFM first compresses the target into weighted atoms using an entropic
Sinkhorn coreset and lifts them to a Gaussian mixture. The induced conditional
velocity law is then a closed-form Gaussian mixture that can be sampled without
a learned neural sampler.
A lightweight correction flow, trained from this exact surrogate source,
then refines the remaining surrogate-to-target residual rather than
learning an entire noise-to-data map.
We prove that the surrogate transport cost equals the
target–surrogate Wasserstein gap under an explicit compression
assumption, whereas the noise-source analogue has a dimension-scale
lower bound. We further characterize the conditional second moment of
the direct surrogate-source training target and show that its
source-dependent excess is small when the surrogate conditional law is
close to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance.
Empirically, on
MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and CelebA-HQ, the proposed method reaches
competitive few-step generation under matched architectures. Codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ccvfm-code-11D3/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow matching [ 17 , 18 , 1 ] has emerged as a simple and competitive paradigm for generative modeling. Given a source X 0 ∼ ρ 0 X_{0}\sim\rho_{0} and a target X 1 ∼ ρ 1 X_{1}\sim\rho_{1} , one interpolates X t = ( 1 − t ) ​ X 0 + t ​ X 1 X_{t}=(1-t)X_{0}+tX_{1} , defines the velocity V = X 1 − X 0 V=X_{1}-X_{0} , and regresses a field u θ ​ ( x , t ) u_{\theta}(x,t) on V V under a squared loss. The minimizer is the conditional mean u ⋆ ​ ( x , t ) = 𝔼 ⁡ ( V ∣ X t = x ) u^{\star}(x,t)=\mathbb{E}(V\mid X_{t}=x) , which suffices to match the marginal evolution but collapses the entire conditional law π ⁡ ( v ∣ x , t ) \pi(v\mid x,t) to a single direction . Whenever the same intermediate state x x is consistent with several endpoint completions, mean-field learning blurs the local transport structure and forces long integration paths (high NFE) at inference to compensate. The NFE cost of few-step generation therefore has a structural component that no amount of solver engineering can remove: the field itself has been averaged. The closest prior attempt to break this bottleneck is the hierarchical rectified flow (HRF2) of Zhang et al. [30] , which models the full conditional law π ⁡ ( v ∣ x , t ) \pi(v\mid x,t) via a second-level flow in velocity space. HRF2 proves a key structural identity: when ρ 1 \rho_{1} is a GMM, the induced conditional velocity law is itself a closed-form GMM [ 30 , Thm. 1 and Cor. 1 of] , and we leverage this identity extensively. Its limitation is the choice of source: the correction flow starts from an isotropic v 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) v_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and must learn the entire transport from noise to a potentially multimodal velocity law, so the correction step carries most of the load and low-NFE generation remains hard. We introduce Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching (CCVFM), which keeps HRF2’s hierarchical structure but replaces its isotropic source with a data-informed surrogate in closed form. Stage I fits K K weighted atoms using entropic Sinkhorn and lifts them to a GMM ρ ~ 1 = ∑ k w k ​ 𝒩 ​ ( μ k , Σ k ) \widetilde{\rho}_{1}=\sum_{k}w_{k}\mathcal{N}({\mu_{k}},\Sigma_{k}) . Stage II plugs ρ ~ 1 \widetilde{\rho}_{1} into the closed-form velocity identity, giving a zero-parameter mixture sampler for π ~ ​ ( v ∣ x , t ) \widetilde{\pi}(v\mid x,t) . Stage III trains a direct surrogate-source correction flow instead of the full noise-to-data map. The theoretical comparison is sharp at the generation boundary t = 0 t=0 , where π ⁡ ( v ∣ x 0 , 0 ) = ρ 1 ​ ( x 0 + v ) \pi(v\mid x_{0},0)=\rho_{1}(x_{0}+v) . The CCVFM correction cost equals W 2 ​ ( ρ 1 , ρ ~ 1 ) W_{2}(\rho_{1},\widetilde{\rho}_{1}) and is O ( K − 1 / d ) O(K^{-1/d}) under our explicit Stage-I compression assumption; the corresponding noise-source cost has a positive dimension-scale lower bound. In addition we characterize the conditional second moment of the Stage III training residual under the direct surrogate-source sampler, which equals tr ⁡ Σ π ​ ( C ) + tr ⁡ Σ sur ​ ( C ) + ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) − μ sur ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 \operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\pi}(C)+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)+\|\mu_{\pi}(C)-\mu_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)\|^{2} , where C = ( X t , t ) C=(X_{t},t) . Its source-dependent excess is small whenever the surrogate conditional law is close to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance, in contrast to the independent-Gaussian-source baseline whose source-dependent excess is ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 + d \|\mu_{\pi}(C)\|^{2}+d .

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (1) We introduce a coreset-to-velocity pipeline that replaces the inner Gaussian source in hierarchical flow matching by a closed-form coreset-GMM surrogate. (2) We prove a transport-task reduction (Theorem 1 ): the CCVFM correction-source cost vanishes with K K under the Stage-I compression assumption, while the HRF2 (noise-source) cost is bounded below by a positive constant in K K and n n . We further establish a direct surrogate-source identity (Theorem 3 ): the Stage-III training source has marginal exactly π ~ ( ⋅ ∣ C ) \widetilde{\pi}(\cdot\mid C) , and its conditional training-residual second moment admits a closed-form expression in the conditional means and covariances of π ( ⋅ ∣ C ) \pi(\cdot\mid C) and π ~ ( ⋅ ∣ C ) \widetilde{\pi}(\cdot\mid C) , whose source-dependent excess is small whenever the surrogate is close to the target in mean and covariance. (3) We obtain strong few-step image results: MNIST FID 50 ​ k = 0.75 {}_{50k}=0.75 , CIFAR-10 FID 50 ​ k = 6.35 {}_{50k}=6.35 , ImageNet-32 FID 50 ​ k = 8.76 {}_{50k}=8.76 , and CelebA-HQ 256 FID 28 ​ k = 4.17 {}_{28k}=4.17 , all at 51 51 NFE. (4) Building on existing nearest-neighbour-based generative-model diagnostics [ 2 , 19 , 3 , 4 ] , we adapt the 1 1 -NN primitive into a 1 1 -NN Inception-feature goodness-of-fit diagnostic showing no preferential closeness to training data.

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: Rectified flow [ 18 ] and conditional flow matching [ 17 ] sample X 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and X 1 ∼ ρ 1 X_{1}\sim\rho_{1} , set X t = ( 1 − t ) ​ X 0 + t ​ X 1 X_{t}=(1-t)X_{0}+tX_{1} , and regress a field on V = X 1 − X 0 V=X_{1}-X_{0} . The optimum 𝔼 ⁡ [ V ∣ X t = x ] \mathbb{E}[V\mid X_{t}=x] matches marginals but discards the full conditional law, which motivates velocity-distribution methods such as HRF2 [ 30 ] . HRF2 learns π ⁡ ( v ∣ x t , t ) \pi(v\mid x_{t},t) through a second flow with Gaussian inner source and uses the identity π ⁡ ( v ∣ x t , t ) ∝ ρ 0 ​ ( x t − t ​ v ) ​ ρ 1 ​ ( x t + ( 1 − t ) ​ v ) , \pi(v\mid x_{t},t)\propto\rho_{0}\big(x_{t}-tv\big)\,\rho_{1}\big(x_{t}+(1-t)v\big), (1) whose GMM specialization gives explicit component means, covariances, and weights whenever ρ 1 \rho_{1} is a GMM. The remaining difficulty is that HRF2’s inner flow starts from isotropic noise and must cross mixture modes. Weighted coresets compress data into atoms { ( w k , μ k ) } k = 1 K \{(w_{k},\mu_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K} that approximate ρ 1 \rho_{1} in transport distance [ 7 , 6 ] . Classical quantization [ 10 ] gives the O ( K − 1 / d ) O(K^{-1/d}) benchmark for globally optimal K K -atomic approximants under standard assumptions. For the deployed entropic-Sinkhorn/GMM output we use the corresponding rate only through the explicit Stage-I compression assumption.

sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: Generative modeling and few-step sampling. GANs [ 9 ] , VAEs [ 15 ] , and normalizing flows [ 22 , 8 ] established the modern toolkit, with tradeoffs in stability, likelihood bounds, or architecture. Score-based diffusion models [ 13 , 26 , 14 ] drive recent image quality but often need long chains; EDM [ 14 ] is the strongest CIFAR-10 efficiency benchmark. Consistency models [ 25 ] and progressive distillation [ 24 ] compress trained teachers, while ReFlow [ 18 ] and mini-batch OT-CFM [ 27 , 21 ] straighten paths. CCVFM is orthogonal: it reduces the inner correction transport before any distillation, straightening, OT coupling, or solver choice. Flow matching and velocity distributions. Conditional flow matching [ 17 ] , rectified flow [ 18 ] , and stochastic interpolants [ 1 , 27 , 21 ] regress the conditional mean velocity, which is the squared-loss optimum but collapses multimodal local velocity laws. The closest prior work is HRF2 [ 30 ] , which models π ⁡ ( v ∣ x t , t ) \pi(v\mid x_{t},t) via a second-level velocity-space flow. We keep HRF2’s identity and closed-form GMM corollary, but replace its 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) source with a coreset-GMM surrogate sampled directly through its conditional mixture weights, so that the training source marginal equals the inference source marginal exactly. Concurrently, Guo and Schwing [11] proposed a variational low-dimensional latent route to velocity multimodality. Coresets, smoothing, and diagnostics. Stage I builds on entropic Optimal Transport (OT) [ 7 ] and weighted coreset / quantization theory [ 6 , 10 , 29 ] . Classical quantization provides the optimal K K -atomic benchmark, while the deployed Sinkhorn / GMM rate is used through the explicit Stage-I compression assumption. Theorem 3 expresses the conditional second moment of the direct surrogate-source training residual in the means and covariances of π ( ⋅ ∣ C ) \pi(\cdot\mid C) and π ~ ( ⋅ ∣ C ) \widetilde{\pi}(\cdot\mid C) ; the independent-Gaussian-source lower bound uses the law of total variance applied to the conditional law π ⁡ ( v ∣ x t , t ) \pi(v\mid x_{t},t) . In our diagnostic, we use improved precision / recall [ 23 , 16 , 20 ] , and an 1 1 -NN KS/ W 1 W_{1} memorization test built on prior nearest-neighbour-based generative-model diagnostics [ 2 , 19 , 3 , 4 ] .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: CCVFM replaces the velocity-space flow’s isotropic noise source with a closed-form coreset-GMM surrogate and trains the correction network from that surrogate source directly. The surrogate gap equals W 2 ​ ( ρ 1 , ρ ~ 1 ) W_{2}(\rho_{1},\widetilde{\rho}_{1}) and vanishes with K K under the Stage-I compression assumption, while the noise-source analogue has a dimension-scale lower bound that is constant in K K and n n (Theorem 1 ). The direct surrogate-source training residual has conditional second moment tr ⁡ Σ π ​ ( C ) + tr ⁡ Σ sur ​ ( C ) + ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) − μ sur ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 \operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\pi}(C)+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)+\|\mu_{\pi}(C)-\mu_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)\|^{2} , whose source-dependent excess is smaller than the independent-Gaussian-source penalty ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 + d \|\mu_{\pi}(C)\|^{2}+d whenever the surrogate is close to the target conditional velocity law in mean and covariance (Theorem 3 ). Limitations include pessimistic high- d d constants, the assumed compression rate for the deployed coreset/GMM, residual-field regularity in the NFE scaling, EDM’s remaining CIFAR-10 lead at matched NFE. Future work should prove algorithmic rates for the entropic-Sinkhorn/GMM stage, extend the surrogate analysis to other target-density classes, and combine CCVFM with distillation/straightening.

sections.text: If ρ 1 \rho_{1} is supported on [ 0 , 1 ] d [0,1]^{d} and the Stage-I coreset ρ ~ 1 , K \widetilde{\rho}_{1,K} is a global K K -atom Wasserstein quantizer, then D ( Q CCVFM ) = W 2 ( ρ 1 , ρ ~ 1 , K ) = O ( K − 1 / d ) D(Q_{\mathrm{CCVFM}})=W_{2}(\rho_{1},\widetilde{\rho}_{1,K})=O(K^{-1/d}) by Theorem 6 (i) and Lemma 8 . This consequence applies to exact global Wasserstein quantization. It does not assert that the finite-iteration entropic-Sinkhorn/GMM routine used in Stage I necessarily returns such a global quantizer. For the deployed routine, the corresponding approximation property is imposed as Assumption 1 of the main paper. Remark 9 (How to read the coreset assumption) . The preceding consequence uses only the W 2 W_{2} approximation property W 2 ( ρ 1 , ρ ~ 1 , K ) = O ( K − 1 / d ) W_{2}(\rho_{1},\widetilde{\rho}_{1,K})=O(K^{-1/d}) . If Stage I is not solved as an exact global quantization problem, it is enough to assume or prove that the returned coreset satisfies the same rate, possibly with additional optimization, entropic-regularization, and GMM-lift slack. This paper treats that deployed-rate statement as the Stage-I compression assumption rather than as a consequence of the algorithm.

sections.heading: D.5 Source-distribution ablation
sections.text: The choice of training source distribution is the central difference between CCVFM and HRF2: CCVFM trains the correction network with source π ~ ( ⋅ ∣ C ) \widetilde{\pi}(\cdot\mid C) , whereas HRF2 uses the isotropic Gaussian 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) . An isolated, matched-recipe ablation that replaces π ~ \widetilde{\pi} by 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) while keeping K K , the architecture, and the training schedule identical is left to future work. In lieu of the matched retrain, Proposition 14 gives an exact identity for the conditional second moment of the training residual under the direct surrogate sampler: 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ V 1 − V 0 ‖ 2 ∣ C ] = tr ⁡ Σ π ​ ( C ) + tr ⁡ Σ sur ​ ( C ) + ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) − μ sur ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 \mathbb{E}[\|V_{1}-V_{0}\|^{2}\mid C]=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\pi}(C)+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)+\|\mu_{\pi}(C)-\mu_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)\|^{2} . The corresponding identity for the independent Gaussian source is tr ⁡ Σ π ​ ( C ) + ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 + d \operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\pi}(C)+\|\mu_{\pi}(C)\|^{2}+d (Proposition 15 ). The surrogate source has a strictly smaller training-target scale whenever tr ⁡ Σ sur ​ ( C ) + ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) − μ sur ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 < ‖ μ π ​ ( C ) ‖ 2 + d \operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)+\|\mu_{\pi}(C)-\mu_{\mathrm{sur}}(C)\|^{2}<\|\mu_{\pi}(C)\|^{2}+d , i.e. when the surrogate conditional law is closer to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance than the isotropic Gaussian source.

sections.heading:
Why Stage III at 1 1 step is no better
(and slightly worse) than Stage II at 1 1 step on these toys.
sections.text: On low-dimensional toys with a clean modal structure (ring-6, moons, pinwheel, helix-3D), the surrogate gap W 2 ​ ( ρ 1 , ρ ~ 1 ) W_{2}(\rho_{1},\widetilde{\rho}_{1}) is already very small at K ∈ { 6 , … , 32 } K\in\{6,\ldots,32\} , so the closed-form Stage II 1 1 -step generator essentially saturates the achievable error: there is little within-mode residual for Stage III to absorb. At a budget of L = 1 L{=}1 inner correction step, the learned residual is then dominated by the stochastic Euler discretization error rather than by a useful systematic correction, which manifests as a small SW 2 increase on moons (0.087 → \to 0.127), pinwheel (0.058 → \to 0.177), and helix-3D (0.035 → \to 0.134). The Stage III correction is designed to reduce the within-mode residual at low NFE when the surrogate gap is non-negligible , which is the regime of Tables 1 and 3 of the main paper; it is not designed to help when Stage II already attains the surrogate floor at 1 1 -step. Increasing L L recovers Stage II’s error level but is not a feature of the toy benchmark.

sections.heading: G.1 Why size-matching matters
sections.text: Nearest-neighbour distances and kernel-based precision/recall are sensitive to pool size: larger reference pools generally produce smaller 1 1 -NN distances, because the probability that any query point finds a nearby neighbour grows with the number of candidates. If we compared 50,000 50{,}000 training images to 10,000 10{,}000 generated images without controlling pool sizes, the training pool would appear artificially closer to the generated pool simply because it has 5 × 5\times more candidates per query. To remove this confound entirely, we enforce a single pool size N pool = 10,000 N_{\text{pool}}=10{,}000 across all three pools (Generated, Test, Training). The 10,000 10{,}000 figure is set by the held-out test set size; we sub-sample the training set uniformly at random to match, and we draw exactly 10,000 10{,}000 generated samples from the Stage III L=20 generator (FID 50 ​ k = 1.09 {}_{50k}=1.09 ).

sections.heading: G.6 Interpretation in plain language
sections.text: The headline message of the goodness-of-fit table is: if you were handed three unlabeled pools of MNIST-like images (one from the true distribution, one sub-sampled from the training set, and one from our generator) and you were asked to detect which pool was synthetic by looking at 1 1 -NN distances to held-out real data, you would fail within the statistical tolerance of an i.i.d. real ↔ \leftrightarrow real baseline. Memorization (generations clustered near specific training images) would produce an asymmetry between Ge → \to Tr and Ge → \to Te distances; we do not observe one. Mode-dropping (generations clustered away from certain real regions) would produce an asymmetry between Ge → \to Te and Te → \to Ge; we do not observe one either. Together with the precision/recall indistinguishability across references, this triangulates goodness of fit more stringently than FID alone can do.

sections.heading: G.7 Caveats
sections.text: Our memorization test probes the Inception feature embedding of MNIST digits; rare sample-level copies that are InceptionV3-close to training images would not be detected if they happen to match the held-out test set equally well in that embedding. A stricter pixel-level duplicate detection (e.g. perceptual-hash collisions) is a useful complementary check; we conducted a preliminary scan on Plan C generations that found no pixel-level duplicates to training images at a 10 − 3 10^{-3} Hamming threshold, but we defer a systematic version of that test to the camera-ready.

Hierarchical flow matching models the full conditional velocity law in velocity space, but its inner flow is asked to transport isotropic Gaussian noise to a multimodal target velocity distribution from scratch. Our key observation is that this inner source can be replaced by a closed-form surrogate built from a coreset of the target. CCVFM first compresses the target into weighted atoms using an entropic Sinkhorn coreset and lifts them to a Gaussian mixture. The induced conditional velocity law is then a closed-form Gaussian mixture that can be sampled without a learned neural sampler. A lightweight correction flow, trained from this exact surrogate source, then refines the remaining surrogate-to-target residual rather than learning an entire noise-to-data map. We prove that the surrogate transport cost equals the target–surrogate Wasserstein gap under an explicit compression assumption, whereas the noise-source analogue has a dimension-scale lower bound. We further characterize the conditional second moment of the direct surrogate-source training target and show that its source-dependent excess is small when the surrogate conditional law is close to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance. Empirically, on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and CelebA-HQ, the proposed method reaches competitive few-step generation under matched architectures.
